title: tokenization-alignment-and-prefetch-budgeting
content:
Summary:

Quick notes from an exploratory investigation into how tokenizer alignment and prefetch budgeting interact with MoE routing and long-context workloads (LLama/Mistral/Qwen mixes). Goal: surface a concrete, low-risk change to the prefetcher and request assembly pipeline that reduces tail latency for mixed-model clusters while keeping GPU memory pressure predictable.

Why this matters (observed problem):
- In mixed workloads (short chat + occasional 16k-32k documents), we see spiky p99s and throughput cliffs when requests span tokenizer chunk boundaries and trigger asymmetric MoE expert fanout.
- Root cause hypothesis: misaligned token boundaries increase the number of KV-cache fragments and cause extra prefetch rounds. On top of that, our current prefetch budget is global per-GPU rather than request-aware, so heavy fragmented requests can starve other requests or cause repeated CPU->GPU IO bursts.

Models & configs tested (summary):
- llama-2-70b: baseline dense, 32k bpe window simulated by concatenation of segments; CPU tokenization with 6 worker threads; single-GPU run (A100 80GB), batch-size equivalent 1 (latency mode).
- mistral-7b: dense long-window variant, multi-CPU tokenization with worker pool; tested with 16k and 24k contexts.
- qwen-14b: larger vocab fragmentation observed; MoE routing overlay (toy routing layer added to simulate sparsity) to test expert fanout behavior.
- Mixed-run: 60% short (<=512 tokens), 30% mid (2k-8k), 10% long (16k-32k) by synthetic trace.

Experimental harness:
- Synthetic traces derived from real production captures anonymized by truncation and reshuffling.
- Measurements captured: CPU tokenize latency, request assembly time, number of prefetch rounds, GPU mem usage, per-layer expert fanout count, end-to-end p50/p95/p99, and throughput during 10-minute ramps.
- Tools: perf sampling on CPU, nvprof-style sampling (internal run-traces), and our in-house request-trace aggregator.

Key observations:
1) Tokenizer alignment multiplies prefetch rounds
   - When client-provided context aligns to internal prefetch chunk size (4k token quantum), typical prefetch rounds = 1.
   - When misaligned by 1-3 tokens (common due to sentence boundaries / user paste), prefetch rounds increased by 1.3x on average; for large long-context requests (>=16k) this jumped to 1.8x.
   - Extra round cost is dominated by CPU->GPU page copies and small kernel startup overheads (not compute).

2) MoE routing amplifies fragmentation pain
   - In runs with simulated MoE gating, misaligned fragments often routed to overlapping expert sets. This created duplicate KV fragments on GPU (same token sequence now mapped to multiple experts across fragments), increasing peak activation memory by ~12-18% in our configs.
   - Duplicate expert touch also increased small-allocation churn, which triggered fragmentation in our allocator and increased ephemeral OOM/eviction occurrences on long ramps.

3) Global prefetch budget is brittle
   - Current global prefetch budget per-GPU (X MB/s cap + Y outstanding fragments) is oblivious to request-level hotness and token length. Long misaligned requests consumed a disproportionate share of outstanding prefetch slots, causing short requests to queue and p99 to spike.

4) CPU tokenization hiccups cause prefetch jitter
   - Tokenization performed on CPU thread pool can produce bursts of tiny fragments (especially for pasted documents with uneven tokenization cost). These bursts frequently coincide with scheduling slices on the GPU and lead to head-of-line blocking.

Quantitative numbers (representative run):
- Mixed-run baseline (no changes): p50=48ms, p95=240ms, p99=1120ms, throughput=210 reqs/min. Peak GPU mem usage=62GB.
- After aligning synthetic inputs to 4k quantum (no prefetch change): p50=46ms, p95=190ms, p99=720ms, throughput=220 reqs/min. Peak GPU mem=60GB.
- After implementing request-aware prefetch budget (see below): p50=47ms, p95=160ms, p99=320ms, throughput=255 reqs/min. Peak GPU mem=63GB (slight increase due to conservative reservation).

Prototype change: request-aware prefetch budgeting (sketch)
- Idea: allocate prefetch slots per-request based on estimated fragment count and request priority. Two components:
  1) estimate_fragments(request) -> cheap heuristic: ceil(tokens / chunk_size) + router_fragment_penalty (based on expected gating fanout).
  2) per-request reservation: min(max_slots_per_request, floor(global_slots * weight(request))). Weight uses a combination of priority (SLO tier), token_count, and historical steady-state reclaim rate.
- Enforcement: token-level prefetch queue with fast path for aligned fragments. Reclaiming: if a request's fragments are idle for >T_reclaim ms, they move to best-effort queue.
- Safety knobs: max_total_slots, per-expert reservation cap (to avoid hogging by MoE-heavy requests).

Why this helps (empiric):
- Reduced head-of-line by preventing large requests from reserving all outstanding prefetch slots.
- Encourages assembling aligned fragments first (fast-path) because aligned fragments estimate = 1 slot. That reduces extra round trips.
- Limits speculative prefetch duplication for MoE cases via per-expert caps.

Micro-optimization follow-ups implemented in prototype:
- Tokenizer-alignment fast path: if tokenization produces fragment_count==1 for a request, bypass prefetch reservation and submit direct. This reduced p95 for aligned short-mid requests by ~20ms.
- Small-buffer coalescing: during CPU->GPU copy stage, coalesce tiny fragment transfers from same request up to 128KB to reduce PCIe overhead. Improved throughput by ~8%.
- Per-expert soft-limit: stop duplicating KV fragments for the same expert when estimated duplicate gain < threshold. Saved ~6% memory in MoE runs.

Observed trade-offs:
- Reservation increases peak reserved memory (we reserve a small extra margin per-request), which increased peak GPU usage slightly. However the p99 improvements were large enough to justify a small memory headroom increase in most cluster profiles.
- Additional bookkeeping on hot path: the prefetch allocator adds a few microseconds of overhead per request assembly. Net latency improved despite this because it reduced blocking later in the pipeline.

Action items / proposed next steps (lightweight roadmap):
1) Roll the request-aware prefetch allocator to staging with a config flag (enable_prefetch_reservations). Monitor p99, throughput, reserved mem, eviction count. Owner: Daniel Park. (1 week)
2) Add tokenization-alignment logging (sampled) to capture how often real inputs are misaligned vs synthetic trace. Owner: Aisha Kapoor. (3 days)
3) Implement soft per-expert duplication cap in runtime allocator (GHPR: redwood/serve#4823) and test with live MoE-like models. Owner: Marina Lopez. (2 weeks)
4) Add a conservative on-deck buffer coalescer to CPU->GPU copy path with adaptive thresholding. Owner: Ethan Zhou. (1 week)
5) Run 72-hour mixed-load soak on dedicated cluster to observe memory fragmentation and evictions before turning on widely. Owner: eng-sre + eng-serving-runtime. (2-3 weeks)

Open questions / unknowns:
- Router gating estimator: how cheaply and reliably can we estimate gating fanout before executing the model? Current estimator relies on recent sampling but cold requests remain noisy. Need ideas for fast gating heuristics that don't require executing full attention pass.
- Multi-GPU distributed KV sharing: reservation across devices is currently per-GPU. For multi-GPU sharded model configs, do we need cross-device coordination to prevent per-GPU starvation? Coordination cost might negate gains.
- Interaction with on-device quantized caching: duplicate fragments in MoE cases might be cheaper if we compress cached activations; worth exploring combined strategy.

Notes for follow-up experiments:
- Capture traces with real user paste events (we suspect paste-heavy inputs have worse misalignment profile than synthetic corpora).
- Test different chunk_size quantums (2k vs 4k) to see alignment sensitivity and memory trade-offs.
- Build micro-benchmark for gating fanout estimator with small warm cached inputs to measure estimator accuracy vs cost.

Rough timeline to safe deploy (if experiments look like staging):
- 0-2 weeks: staging flag + telemetry + logs.
- 2-6 weeks: per-expert caps + coalescing + extended soak.
- 6-12 weeks: config rollout to canary fleets, then gradual ramp to production clusters.

Appendix: quick trace excerpts (anonymized)
- Example problematic request A: token_count=16423, fragment_count=5 (misaligned), prefetch_rounds=3, observed p99 contribution=480ms, duplicate_expert_touch=4 experts duplicated.
- Example aligned request B: token_count=16384, fragment_count=4 (aligned), prefetch_rounds=1, p99 contribution=32ms.

Closing thoughts:
This felt like a medium-effort / high-impact surface: most of the work is in the allocator and telemetry rather than model code or heavy kernel work. The principle of making prefetch budgeting request-aware seems robust across the Llama/Mistral/Qwen mixes we tried and will be helpful once we onboard more MoE-based variants into the fleet.

Comments welcome — feel free to add experiment notes below or link any existing traces.
